newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican tequila war threatens to halt production.
newsitem.headline: Mexican tequila war threatens to halt production.

text.p: A bitter dispute is smoldering between Mexican agave-growers and tequila-makers that is threatening to halt production of Mexico's famed and potent liquor.
The agave is the cactus-like plant used to make tequila in the western city of Tequila, where eight companies dominate the domestic and export market.
At the core of the dispute is the price tequila-makers are willing to pay for agave.
Angry over what they consider strong-arm tactics by the distillers, hundreds of agave-growers have blocked four roads leading to Tequila since Wednesday, picking and choosing who gets to come and go.

"The blockade is for various reason," Raul Tijerina, a militant of the El Barzon Agavero debtors' group organizing the protest, said in an interview. "The agave is rotting in the fields, the prices are too low and it takes us nine years to make it."

Tijerina spoke from the roadblock at the main entrance to Tequila, where trucks filled with agave were forced to park in a soccer field at the side of the road. About 400 protesters have camped out with several of the women agave-growers taking turns cooking.

The tequila makers say there is a glut of agave, plain and simple, and are appalled at the growers' strong-arm tactics, which if they continue past Friday could totally shut down production, one factory manager said.

But the growers allege a conspiracy to drive down prices and charge that exporters are cheating foreign customers by making tequila with a miniumum of agave and making up the rest with cheaper products like sugar.

The government is attempting to mediate the dispute, but the impasse grew worse on Thursday when the producers failed to show for a scheduled meeting between the two sides, demanding that the growers first reopen the road and allow the detained trucks to pass.

Rene Beas, leader of the agave growers, said they allowed 12 of 16 detained trucks to pass through on Friday as a measure of good faith but that they will not end their blockade. Normally, about 40 trucks a day enter Tequila, according to local media reports.
"If we open the road, they're going to start producing all day long, 2,000 or 3,000 tons, and gain another 10 or 15 days' time," Beas said.
Beas said the 12 trucks that passed contained agave, but the other four that were held up carried sugar.
"Sugar is replacing the original raw material (agave) of authentic tequila," said Joaquin Romero, the legal adviser for the Regional Agricultural Union of Agave Producers.
Added Beas, "We can't let them keep putting sugar in tequila."
Benjamin Garcia Duran, plant manager for Tequila Cuervo, which exports its product under the Jose Cuervo brand name, said if blockade extends past Friday, it would affect production by "100 percent."
"Each day of the stoppage prevents us from producing 50,000 liters of tequila," he said.
Garcia Duran said more than 90 percent of Cuervo's daily production of 320 tons is destined for export.

Meanwhile, as long as the road is blocked, agave producers cannot sell their product, no matter what the price. But they said they might strike back by producing their own brand of tequila, making it the old-fashioned way - in backyard wooden vats instead of modern factories.
"We've have a little distillery where tequila is made the traditional way, and it's very profitable for us," said Julian Rodriguez of El Barzon. "We're making about 1,600 bottles a week."
